# Cūḷasaccaka Sutta (MN 35 (PTS MN i 227))

**ID:** MN 35 (PTS MN i 227)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Cūḷasaccaka Sutta
**PTS:** MN i 227
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0201m.mul3.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Cūḷasaccaka Sutta* ("The Shorter Discourse With Saccaka", MN 35) is the thirty-fifth discourse of the Majjhimanikāya, set in the Mahāvana forest outside Vesālī [Buswell & Lopez 2014]. In this discourse, Saccaka, the son of Nigaṇṭha (Jain) parents who is addressed by the clan name Aggivessana, boasts of his skill as a debater and challenges the Buddha to a philosophical contest [Buswell & Lopez 2014; Galasek 2016; Jamspal 1991]. Saccaka asserts that the five aggregates (*khandha*) constitute the permanent self (*attā* / *ātman*) [Buswell & Lopez 2014; Jamspal 1991]. The Buddha systematically refutes this position by demonstrating that the aggregates are impermanent (*anicca*), unsatisfactory (*dukkha*), and outside autonomous control, thereby establishing the teaching of not-self (*anattā*) [Buswell & Lopez 2014; Kuznetsova et al. 2012]. During the debate, King Ajātasattu is cited as an example of monarchical authority [Radich 2011], and the Buddha remarks on his ability to sit motionless for days experiencing supreme bliss [Polak 2011]. When Saccaka twice refuses to respond to a question, he is compelled to answer under the threat of the yakkha Vajirapāṇī shattering his head [Gergely, Mahā-Daṇḍadhāraṇī-Śītavatī; Galasek 2016]. Following his defeat, Saccaka hosts the Buddha and the monastic community for a meal [Jamspal 1991]. The sutta is also referenced in several debates of the *Kathāvatthu* (Kv 1.1, Kv 2.8, Kv 23.5).

Full parallels to the discourse are preserved in the Chinese Āgamas (*Saṁyukta-āgama* SĀ 110 and *Ekottarika-āgama* EĀ 37.10), Sanskrit fragments (SHT sutta 34), and the Tibetan *Upāyikā* (Up 6.005) [Anālayo 2014].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Full parallels: EA 37.10; SA 110 薩遮; SHT Sutta 34
- Resembling parallels: SN 22.15 Yadaniccasutta; SA 10 無常; SA 9 無常; SN 22.16 Yaṁdukkhasutta; SN 22.17 Yadanattāsutta; Up 6.005
- Mentioned in: Kv 23.5 Aparinipphannakathā; Kv 2.8 Kukkuḷakathā; Kv 1.1 Puggalakathā

**Sources**

- [Buswell & Lopez 2014] Robert E. Buswell Jr. and Donald S. Lopez Jr., Princeton Dictionary of Buddhism (2014) — Supplied setting, discourse outline, and the debate over the aggregates, impermanence, and suffering.
- [Galasek 2016] Bruno Galasek, On Presenting Characters and Representation of Persons... (2016) — Detailed Saccaka's reluctance to respond and the Buddha's warning to answer.
- [Gergely, Mahā-Daṇḍadhāraṇī-Śītavatī] Gergely, Mahā-Daṇḍadhāraṇī-Śītavatī: A Buddhist Apotropaic Scripture — Discussed the motif of Vajirapāṇī threatening to split the head of someone who fails to answer a question.
- [Jamspal 1991] Lozang Jamspal, The Range of the Bodhisattva (1991) — Described Saccaka's background, the address Aggivessana, his view on ātman, and the subsequent meal offering.
- [Kuznetsova et al. 2012] Irina Kuznetsova, Jonardon Ganeri, and Chakravarthi Ram-Prasad, Hindu and Buddhist Ideas in Dialogue (2012) — Contextualized the debate with Saccaka regarding self and not-self among non-Brahmin interlocutors.
- [Polak 2011] Grzegorz Polak, Reexamining Jhana (2011) — Noted the Buddha's ability to remain seated motionless for days experiencing bliss.
- [Radich 2011] Michael Radich, How Ajātasattu Was Reformed (2011) — Noted the brief reference to King Ajātasattu in the discourse.
- [Anālayo 2014] Bhikkhu Anālayo, Perspectives on Satipaṭṭhāna (2014) — Cited scholarly study of the Saṁyukta-āgama parallel to the discourse.
